mcqs.q: Working length is defined as:
opts: The distance from a coronal reference point to the point at which canal preparation and obturation should terminate
The distance from the apical constriction to the apical foramen
The length of the file used to negotiate the canal
The distance from the gingival margin to the radiographic apex
mcqs.explain: Two aspects therefore matter: the coronal reference point and the apical end of the preparation and obturation.

mcqs.q: In the sequence of root canal treatment, working length determination comes:
opts: After access cavity preparation and before cleaning and shaping
Before rubber dam application
After obturation
Before diagnosis and treatment planning
mcqs.explain: Every instrument used from that point on must stop at a length already measured.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the significances of working length?
opts: It determines the taper of the final preparation
It determines how deeply tissues, debris and metabolites are removed
It limits the depth to which the canal filling may be placed
It affects the degree of pain and discomfort following the appointment
mcqs.explain: The best long-term prognosis is observed when the optimum working length is achieved.

mcqs.q: A working length that is too LONG can lead to:
opts: Perforation through the apical constriction and over-extension
Incomplete cleaning and underfilling
Persistent apical periodontitis from retained tissue
A shortened healing period
mcqs.explain: It also causes increased post-operative pain, a prolonged healing period and a lower success rate.

mcqs.q: The lower success rate of an over-long working length is attributed to:
opts: Incomplete regeneration of cementum, periodontal ligament and alveolar bone
Retention of infected pulp tissue in the apical third
Failure of the coronal seal
Fracture of the instrument
mcqs.explain: This is the specific mechanism given for the over-long error.

mcqs.q: A SHORT working length can lead to all the following EXCEPT:
opts: Overfilling
Incomplete cleaning
Persistent discomfort
Apical periodontitis developing and/or persisting
mcqs.explain: Overfilling is a consequence of a working length that is too long; a short length causes underfilling.

mcqs.q: The reference point is:
opts: The site on the occlusal or incisal surface from which measurements are made
The narrowest point of the apical canal
The point at which cementum and dentine unite
The main apical opening of the canal
mcqs.explain: It is used throughout canal preparation and obturation and must not change during or between appointments.

mcqs.q: The reference point is usually taken as:
opts: The highest point on the incisal edge of anterior teeth and a cusp tip on posterior teeth
The gingival margin on all teeth
The deepest point of the access cavity
The contact point with the adjacent tooth
mcqs.explain: It must be stable and easily visualized during preparation.

mcqs.q: A reference point may be created:
opts: By reduction or by elevation
Only by reduction
Only by elevation
Only by placing a composite marker
mcqs.explain: This is done when the existing surface cannot fulfil the four criteria.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the four criteria of a reference point?
opts: It should be the highest cusp in the arch
It should be flat
It should be stable and reproducible
It should be on sound tooth structure
mcqs.explain: All caries, defective restoration and undermined enamel must be removed BEFORE working length determination.

mcqs.q: Why must the reference point be stable?
opts: Because it must not deteriorate with time, since treatment may extend over several visits
Because the rubber dam clamp rests on it
Because it must resist occlusal loading
Because the radiograph is taken from it
mcqs.explain: Reproducibility ensures the working length stays consistent between appointments.

mcqs.q: Rubber stoppers come in thicknesses of:
opts: 0.5 and 1 mm
1 and 2 mm
0.25 and 0.5 mm
2 and 3 mm
mcqs.explain: They also come in different shapes and colours, and include the safety memory disk.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the rubber stopper is correct?
opts: Its position must be re-checked frequently because it can move during insertion and withdrawal of files
A stopper from a large file works equally well on a small file
It should be slightly rounded rather than flat
It should be set 1 mm coronal to the reference point
mcqs.explain: It must remain in intimate contact with the reference point.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the five apical landmarks?
opts: The pulp horn
The anatomic apex
The cemento-dentinal junction
The apical constriction
mcqs.explain: The fifth is the apical foramen.

mcqs.q: The anatomic apex is:
opts: The tip or end of the root determined morphologically, which can only be determined after extraction
The end of the root as seen on a radiograph
The region where dentin and cementum unite
The narrowest point of the apical canal
mcqs.explain: There is no clinical approach to identify it.

mcqs.q: Why can the radiographic apex NOT be used as the apical end of preparation?
opts: Adopting it frequently leads to over-instrumentation
It cannot be seen on a radiograph
It is a histological landmark
It is always more than 3 mm from the constriction
mcqs.explain: Its location can vary from the anatomic apex due to root morphology and distortion of the radiographic image.

mcqs.q: The cemento-dentinal junction is:
opts: The region at which the dentin and cementum are united
The main apical opening of the root canal
The narrowest diameter of the apical canal
The tip of the root seen radiographically
mcqs.explain: It is considered the ideal apical end for preparation and obturation.

mcqs.q: The CDJ is located:
opts: 0.5–3 mm short of the anatomic apex
0.5–1 mm beyond the apical foramen
Exactly at the radiographic apex
3–5 mm short of the apical constriction
mcqs.explain: It does not always coincide with the apical constriction.

mcqs.q: Why can the CDJ not be used clinically as the apical end?
opts: It is a histological landmark that cannot be detected clinically or radiographically
It is always beyond the apical foramen
It does not exist in permanent teeth
It moves during instrumentation
mcqs.explain: This is the central paradox: the ideal landmark is the one that cannot be found in a living patient.

mcqs.q: The apical foramen is also called the:
opts: Major apical diameter
Minor apical diameter
Cemento-dentinal junction
Anatomic apex
mcqs.explain: The apical constriction is the minor apical diameter.

mcqs.q: The apical foramen is frequently located:
opts: Eccentrically, away from the anatomic or radiographic apex
Exactly at the anatomic apex
Coronal to the apical constriction
Within the cemento-dentinal junction itself
mcqs.explain: It connects the pulp with the surrounding bone and contains neural, vascular and connective elements.

mcqs.q: Deviation of the apical foramen increases with:
opts: Aging, consequent to cementum deposition, and differs with tooth type
Caries progression
Pulp vitality
Occlusal loading only
mcqs.explain: External root resorption could alter the shape of the apical foramen and might even eliminate it.

mcqs.q: The apical constriction is:
opts: The apical portion of the root canal having the narrowest diameter
The main apical opening of the canal
The junction of cementum and dentine
The flared portion between the minor and major diameters
mcqs.explain: It is also called the minor apical diameter.

mcqs.q: The apical constriction is usually located:
opts: 0.5–1.0 mm short of the apical foramen
0.5–1.0 mm beyond the apical foramen
2–3 mm short of the apical foramen
Exactly at the radiographic apex
mcqs.explain: Its position may vary, and a few studies have reported a total lack of the AC.

mcqs.q: Cementum deposition with aging causes:
opts: An increase in the distance between the AC and the radiographic apex
A decrease in the distance between the AC and the radiographic apex
Complete obliteration of the apical foramen in all cases
No change in apical anatomy
mcqs.explain: This is why the funnel between the minor and major diameters widens with age.

mcqs.q: The space between the major and minor apical diameters has been described as:
opts: Funnel-shaped, hyperbolic, or the shape of a morning glory flower
Cylindrical
Hourglass-shaped
Spherical
mcqs.explain: From the AC the canal widens as it approaches the AF.

mcqs.q: According to Kuttler's study (JADA 1955), the distance between the major and minor diameters at 18–25 years is:
opts: 0.5 mm exactly
1.0 mm
mcqs.explain: At 55 years and over it is 0.659 mm.

mcqs.q: According to Kuttler, the distance between the major and minor diameters at 55 years and over is:
opts: 0.5 mm
1.5 mm
mcqs.explain: The increase with age is a consequence of continued cementum deposition.

mcqs.q: According to Ingle, the ideal apical termination for root canal preparation is the:
opts: Cemento-dentinal junction
Radiographic apex
Apical foramen
Anatomic apex
mcqs.explain: Considerable controversy nonetheless exists over the exact termination point.

mcqs.q: The lecture's summary statement about the apical part of the root canal is that:
opts: Its most consistent feature is inconsistency or variability
It is remarkably uniform between teeth
It can always be located with a radiograph
It is identical in all age groups
mcqs.explain: This is why no single landmark can be used reliably.

mcqs.q: For most cases, the file tip is placed at:
opts: 0.5–1 mm coronal to the radiographic apex
At the radiographic apex
1–2 mm beyond the radiographic apex
2–3 mm coronal to the radiographic apex
mcqs.explain: This increases the chances of terminating cleaning and shaping inside the canal, in the vicinity of the AC and AF.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the prerequisites of working length determination?
opts: Completion of the obturation of adjacent canals
Knowledge of pulp anatomy and the average length of each root
Straight-line access and coronal pre-flaring
Use of K-files for canal negotiation
mcqs.explain: The other prerequisites are knowledge of armamentarium, good undistorted preoperative radiographs, and a proper reference point noted in the record.

mcqs.q: The four parts of an electronic apex locator are:
opts: The lip clip, the file clip, the electronic device and the connecting cord
The probe, the display, the battery and the charger
The lip clip, the probe, the ruler and the cord
The file, the stopper, the gauge and the device
mcqs.explain: The cord connects the other three parts.

mcqs.q: Who first reported the use of electric current to measure root canal working length?
opts: Custer, in 1918
Suzuki, in 1942
Sunada, in 1962
Huang, in 1987
mcqs.explain: Suzuki revisited the idea in 1942 and Sunada created a device in 1962.

mcqs.q: Who found that an electrode on the oral mucosa and an instrument in the root canal gave consistent measurements of electrical resistance?
opts: Suzuki, in 1942
Custer, in 1918
Sunada, in 1962
Kuttler, in 1955
mcqs.explain: Sunada then used this principle in 1962 to create a direct-current device.

mcqs.q: Huang, in 1987, suggested that the principle of electronic apex locators:
opts: Does not depend on the resistance of biological tissues, but rather on physics
Depends entirely on tissue resistance
Requires alternating current only
Works only in necrotic pulps
mcqs.explain: EALs have been under multiple developments and improvements since then.

mcqs.q: How does an EAL function?
opts: By using the human body to complete an electrical circuit, which closes when the file tip touches periodontal tissue at the apex
By measuring the ultrasonic echo from the apex
By detecting the change in temperature at the apex
By measuring the resistance of the gutta-percha
mcqs.explain: One side is connected to the oral mucosa through a lip clip and the other to a file.

mcqs.q: Why do apex locators NOT replace radiographs?
opts: Their accuracy varies from 55 to 93%, false readings may occur, and check films add information on canal width, curvature and the relationship of multiple canals
They cannot be used under rubber dam
They give no numerical reading
They cannot be used on posterior teeth
mcqs.explain: It is recommended to use an apex locator with the radiographic technique.

mcqs.q: In using an EAL, the file size chosen should be:
opts: Compatible with the canal size — the IAF, the largest file that reaches the full working length
The smallest file available
A size 40 file in every case
A rotary nickel-titanium file
mcqs.explain: The chamber and canals should also be neither too dry nor too wet.

mcqs.q: During EAL use, the reading should be confirmed stable at the:
opts: 0.5 mark
1.0 mark
APEX mark exactly
2.0 mark
mcqs.explain: The rubber stopper is then adjusted to the reference point before the file is removed.

mcqs.q: Which is a cause of a FALSE POSITIVE reading?
opts: Contact of the device with a metal filling
Calcified root canals
Apical blockage by dentin debris
A canal that is too dry
mcqs.explain: False positives arise when the current finds an unintended path to the tissues — metal, saliva, lateral canals, perforation, an open apex, or a canal that is too wet.

mcqs.q: Which is a cause of a FALSE NEGATIVE reading?
opts: Residual root canal filling material in retreatment cases
Contact with saliva
Lateral canals
An open apex
mcqs.explain: False negatives arise when the current cannot get through at all — calcification, blockage, dryness, low batteries or an incomplete circuit.

mcqs.q: Which is listed among the ADVANTAGES of the apex locator?
opts: 80–97% accuracy observed, with much less time required
Accuracy is independent of apex maturity
It replaces the need for radiographs entirely
It is unaffected by battery charge
mcqs.explain: The devices are also mobile, lightweight and easy to use, and reduce additional radiation, which is particularly useful in pregnancy.

mcqs.q: Apex locators are particularly useful in which patients?
opts: Patients with a gag reflex who cannot tolerate X-ray films, children, disabled patients and heavily sedated patients
Patients with cardiac pacemakers
Patients with open apices
Patients with extensive periapical lesions
mcqs.explain: Pacemakers, open apices and extensive periapical lesions are all limitations rather than indications.

mcqs.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of the apex locator?
opts: Accuracy is limited to mature root apices
It requires a long treatment time
It cannot be used with rubber dam
It increases radiation exposure
mcqs.explain: Extensive periapical lesions can give faulty readings, weak batteries affect accuracy, and it can interfere with artificial cardiac pacemakers.

mcqs.q: Apex locators must be used cautiously in patients with:
opts: Artificial cardiac pacemakers
Diabetes mellitus
Hypertension
Asthma
mcqs.explain: They can interfere with the functioning of the pacemaker.

mcqs.q: Regarding moisture, the canal during EAL use should be:
opts: Relatively dry — neither too wet nor too dry
Completely dry
Flooded with irrigant
Filled with blood
mcqs.explain: Both extremes are listed among the factors affecting accuracy.

mcqs.q: Why should pulpal tissue remnants be minimized before accepting an apex reading?
opts: Intact vital tissue, inflammatory exudates and blood conduct electric current and cause inaccurate readings
They block the file mechanically
They dissolve the lip clip
They increase the battery drain
mcqs.explain: The canal should also be free from debris, since lack of patency and dentine debris affect accurate WL determination.

mcqs.q: Regarding irrigants, the lecture states that:
opts: The majority of present-generation apex locators are not affected by irrigants, and the Root ZX is more accurate in the presence of sodium hypochlorite
All apex locators give false readings in any irrigant
Irrigants must be removed completely before any reading
Only saline may be present in the canal
mcqs.explain: This is a specific finding noted for the Root ZX.

mcqs.q: Apex locators are correctly described as:
opts: Apical AREA locators — of the constriction or foramen — rather than root canal length “calculators”
Precise calculators of total root canal length
Devices that measure canal curvature
Devices that measure canal diameter
mcqs.explain: This is particularly helpful when the apex is superimposed on anatomical structures, making a radiograph impossible to use.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the other uses of apex locators?
opts: To measure the taper of the prepared canal
To detect root perforations to clinically acceptable limits
To detect horizontal fractures
To recognize connections between the root canal and the periodontal membrane such as fracture, cracks and resorption
mcqs.explain: They can also determine the location of root and pulpal floor perforations and confirm suspected perforations during post-space preparation.

mcqs.q: In the summary, the appropriate and reliable endpoint for root canal treatment is stated to be the:
opts: Apical constriction
Radiographic apex
Anatomic apex
Apical foramen
mcqs.explain: The CDJ is the practical and anatomic termination point, but it cannot be determined clinically or radiographically.

mcqs.q: Modern apex locators can determine the apical constriction with accuracies:
opts: Greater than 90%, but with some limitations
Of exactly 100%
Below 50%
Only in anterior teeth
mcqs.explain: All generations can be equally useful and accurate in determining working length.

mcqs.q: The overall conclusion regarding methods of WL determination is that:
opts: No individual method is truly satisfactory, so a combination of methods should be used
The EAL alone is always sufficient
The radiograph alone is always sufficient
Tactile sensation alone is the most reliable method
mcqs.explain: This is why the clinical protocol combines the preoperative radiograph, the EAL and a confirmatory periapical film.

mcqs.q: In the clinical WL protocol, the length is confirmed with:
opts: A periapical radiograph taken by the paralleling technique
A panoramic radiograph
A bitewing radiograph
A second EAL reading only
mcqs.explain: If the adjustment needed is greater than ±2 mm, the PA is retaken.

mcqs.q: The PA should be retaken if the adjustment needed is greater than:
opts: ±2 mm
±1 mm
±5 mm
mcqs.explain: This protocol reduces the number of acquired radiographs and thus radiation exposure (ESE 2006).

mcqs.q: According to Kim-Park et al. (2008), what percentage of EAL readings were within ±0.5 mm of the apical constriction?
mcqs.explain: Confirming the EAL reading with a periapical radiograph raised this figure to 96%.

mcqs.q: According to Kim-Park et al. (2008), confirming the EAL reading with a PA raised the accuracy figure to:
mcqs.explain: This is the evidence behind combining the two methods rather than relying on either alone.

mcqs.q: How does the laboratory WL protocol differ from the clinical one?
opts: The EAL step is omitted
The preoperative radiograph step is omitted
Preflaring is omitted
The confirmatory PA is omitted
mcqs.explain: An extracted tooth mounted in the lab cannot complete the body's electrical circuit.

mcqs.q: Which combination correctly pairs a landmark with its status as an apical endpoint?
opts: CDJ — ideal but histological and undetectable; radiographic apex — leads to over-instrumentation
CDJ — easily located radiographically; radiographic apex — the ideal endpoint
Apical foramen — perfectly consistent; anatomic apex — clinically identifiable
Apical constriction — always 2 mm from the foramen; CDJ — always at the apex
mcqs.explain: The apical foramen and apical constriction are both described as inconsistent and unreliable apical end levels.

saqs.q: Define working length and explain its significance.
saqs.a: Working length is defined as the distance from a coronal reference point to the point at which canal preparation and obturation should terminate. Hence two aspects are important while determining it: the coronal reference point, and the apical end of the preparation and obturation. Its significance is that it determines how far into the canal the instruments are placed and worked, and thus how deeply the tissues, debris and metabolites are removed; it limits the depth to which the canal filling may be placed; it affects the degree of pain and discomfort that the patient will feel following the appointment; if calculated within correct limits it plays an important role in determining the success of the treatment, and conversely if calculated incorrectly it may cause the treatment to fail; and based on many studies the best long-term prognosis is observed when the optimum working length is achieved.

saqs.q: What are the consequences of failing to accurately determine and maintain the working length?
saqs.a: A length that is too long can lead to perforation through the apical constriction; overfilling or over-extension; an increased incidence of post-operative pain; a prolonged healing period; and a lower success rate, owing to incomplete regeneration of cementum, periodontal ligament and alveolar bone. A short working length can lead to incomplete cleaning; underfilling; persistent discomfort; apical periodontitis developing and/or persisting; and a lower success rate.

saqs.q: Define the reference point and list its criteria.
saqs.a: The reference point is the site on the occlusal or incisal surface from which measurements are made. This point is used throughout canal preparation and obturation and will not change during or between appointments. A reference point is chosen that is stable and easily visualized during preparation; usually this is the highest point on the incisal edge on anterior teeth and a cusp tip on posterior teeth. You may need to create your reference point, either by reduction or by elevation. Its criteria are that it should be flat; it should be stable, meaning it does not deteriorate with time because treatment may be carried out over several visits; it should be reproducible, so that the working length is consistent; and it should be on sound tooth structure, so all caries, defective restoration and undermined enamel must be removed before working length determination. Sometimes a reference point needs to be created to fulfil these four conditions.

saqs.q: Describe the rubber stopper and the rules for its use.
saqs.a: The rubber stopper comes in different shapes and colours and in different thicknesses, 0.5 and 1 mm, and includes the safety memory disk. A stable and flat rubber stopper should be used. Sometimes the rubber stopper moves during the insertion and withdrawal of files, so its position on the file must be re-checked frequently so that it stays in intimate contact with the reference point. A rubber stopper from a large file should not be used on a small file.

saqs.q: List the apical landmarks and explain why each can or cannot be used as the apical end of preparation.
saqs.a: Several landmarks exist at the apical end of the canals: the anatomic apex, the radiographic apex, the cemento-dentinal junction, the apical foramen and the apical constriction. The anatomic apex is the tip or end of the root determined morphologically; it can only be determined after extraction and there is no clinical approach to identify it. The radiographic apex is the tip or end of the root as determined radiographically, and its location can vary from the anatomic apex due to root morphology and distortion of the radiographic image; adopting it as the apical end will frequently lead to over-instrumentation, so it cannot be used. The cemento-dentinal junction is the region at which the dentin and cementum are united; it does not always coincide with the apical constriction and is located 0.5 to 3 mm short of the anatomic apex, and it is considered the ideal apical end for preparation and obturation, but variations in its position have been reported and a few studies reported a total lack of CDJ, cementum extension could be unequal on both sides, and unfortunately it is a histological landmark that cannot be detected clinically or radiographically, so it cannot be used. The apical foramen, the major apical diameter, is the main apical opening of the root canal; it is frequently eccentrically located away from the anatomic or radiographic apex, connects the pulp with the surrounding bone and contains neural, vascular and connective elements, variability in its position has been reported, the prevalence of deviation increases with aging and differs with tooth type consequent to cementum deposition, and external root resorption could alter its shape or even eliminate it, so it is an inconsistent and unreliable apical end level. The apical constriction, the minor apical diameter, is the apical portion of the root canal having the narrowest diameter, usually 0.5 to 1.0 mm short of the apical foramen; variability in its shape has been reported with a few reporting its total lack, cementum deposition with aging increases the distance between it and the radiographic apex, and we still lack a clinical approach that consistently locates it, so it too is an inconsistent and unreliable apical end level.

saqs.q: Describe the relationship between the apical constriction and the apical foramen, and state what is considered an adequate working length.
saqs.a: From the apical constriction, the minor apical diameter, the canal widens as it approaches the apical foramen, the major apical diameter. The space between the major and minor diameters has been described as funnel-shaped, or hyperbolic, or the shape of a morning glory flower. The distance between the major and minor diameters is 0.524 mm at 18 to 25 years and 0.659 mm at 55 years and over, according to Kuttler's study in JADA 1955. According to Ingle, the CDJ has been recommended as the ideal apical termination for root canal preparation, but considerable controversy exists over the exact termination point for cleaning and shaping, because the most consistent feature of the apical part of the root canal is inconsistency or variability. Therefore, for most of the cases, the file tip is placed at 0.5 to 1 mm coronal to the radiographic apex, which increases the chances of terminating cleaning and shaping inside the root canal in the vicinity of the apical constriction and the apical foramen.

saqs.q: List the prerequisites of working length determination.
saqs.a: Knowledge of pulp anatomy and the average length of each individual root. Knowledge of all armamentarium needed. Good quality preoperative radiographs, good and undistorted, showing the total length and all roots of the involved tooth. A proper reference point, a fact that should be noted on the patient's record. Straight-line access. Coronal pre-flaring, with adequate coronal access to all canals. And the use of K-files for canal negotiation.

saqs.q: Describe the electronic apex locator — its parts, its history, and how it works.
saqs.a: The EAL has four parts: the lip clip, the file clip, the electronic device, and the cord which connects the above three parts. Historically, the first reported use of electric current to measure root canal working length was in 1918 by Custer; the idea was revisited by Suzuki in 1942, who found that an electrode placed on the oral mucosa and an instrument placed in the root canal gave consistent measurements of electrical resistance; Sunada in 1962 used this principle to create a device, using direct current, to estimate the root canal length in vivo; and Huang in 1987 suggested that the principle of electronic apex locators does not depend on the resistance of biological tissues but rather on the physics. EALs function by using the human body to complete an electrical circuit: one side of the apex locator's circuit is connected to the oral mucosa through a lip clip and the other side to a file, and when the file is placed into the root canal and advanced apically until its tip touches periodontal tissue at the apex, the electrical circuit is completed. Electronic apex locators are now considered the most ideal method to measure the working length of a root canal, and it is recommended to use an apex locator together with the radiographic technique.

saqs.q: Why do apex locators not replace radiographs?
saqs.a: The apex locator is a useful adjunct in locating the terminus of the canal during root canal treatment, but it does not replace the need for radiographs, because the ability of apex locators to accurately locate the apex varies from 55 to 93%; because that may lead to false readings; and because the need for radiographic check films is essential to add information including canal width, degree of canal curvature, and the relationship of multiple canals within the same root.

saqs.q: List the causes of false positive and false negative readings with an apex locator.
saqs.a: False positive readings may be caused by contact of the device with a metal filling; the presence of pulpal tissue remnant; contact with saliva; lateral canals; perforation; an open apex; and a canal that is too wet. False negative readings may be caused by calcified root canals; residual root canal filling material in retreatment cases; apical blockage by dentin debris; a canal that is too dry; low batteries; and an incomplete circuit.

saqs.q: List the advantages and disadvantages of the apex locator, and the factors affecting its accuracy.
saqs.a: The advantages are that the devices are mobile, lightweight and easy to use; much less time is required; additional radiation to the patient can be reduced, which is particularly useful in cases of pregnancy; 80 to 97% accuracy has been observed; and they can be used in patients with a gag reflex who cannot tolerate X-ray films, and are also useful in children, disabled patients and heavily sedated patients. The disadvantages are that accuracy is limited to mature root apices; extensive periapical lesions can give faulty readings; weak batteries can affect accuracy; and they can interfere with the functioning of artificial cardiac pacemakers, so cautious use is needed in such patients. The factors affecting accuracy are low batteries; an incomplete circuit; the presence of pulpal tissue remnant, since intact vital tissue, inflammatory exudates and blood can conduct electric current and cause inaccurate readings so their presence should be minimized before accepting the apex reading; the presence of perforation or an open apex; a canal that is too wet or too dry, as the canal should be relatively dry; and the presence of blockage from calcification of canals, as the canal should be free from debris and lack of patency with accumulation of dentine debris can affect accurate working length determination. The majority of present-generation apex locators are not affected by irrigants within the root canal, and the Root ZX has been found to be more accurate in the presence of sodium hypochlorite.

saqs.q: State the uses of apex locators.
saqs.a: These devices are not root canal length calculators; rather they are apical area locators, of the constriction or foramen, and this feature can be particularly helpful when the apex is superimposed on anatomical structures, thus making it impossible to use a radiograph. Their other uses are to detect root perforations to clinically acceptable limits; to determine the location of root and pulpal floor perforations; to detect horizontal fractures; to confirm suspected periodontal or pulpal perforations during post-space preparation; and to recognize any connection between the root canal and the periodontal membrane, such as root fracture, cracks, and internal or external resorption.

saqs.q: Give the recommended protocol for working length determination in the clinic and in the laboratory.
saqs.a: In the clinic: first, estimate the working length from the preoperative periapical radiograph; second, ensure preflaring; third, utilize the electronic apex locator; fourth, utilize the supplementary approaches wisely as needed; fifth, confirm the length with a periapical radiograph taken by the paralleling technique; and sixth, if the adjustment needed is greater than plus or minus 2 mm, retake the periapical radiograph. This reduces the number of acquired radiographs and thus reduces radiation exposure, according to the ESE 2006. Kim-Park and colleagues in 2008 found that 84% of EAL readings were within plus or minus 0.5 mm of the apical constriction, and that confirming the EAL reading with a periapical radiograph raised this figure to 96%. In the laboratory the same sequence is used without the apex locator step: estimate the working length from the preoperative periapical radiograph; ensure preflaring; utilize the supplementary approaches wisely as needed; confirm the length with a periapical radiograph taken by the paralleling technique; and if the adjustment needed is greater than plus or minus 2 mm, retake the periapical radiograph.
